claims.claim: Depletion of SUMO in female germline caused changes in gene expression.
claims.source: In agreement with known role of SUMO in Pol II transcription, its depletion in female germline caused changes in gene expression.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis in the current study.

claims.claim: SUMO depletion caused statistically significant >2 fold up-regulation of ~4% (323) and down-regulation of ~1.5% (138) of the analyzed genes.
claims.source: We observed statistically significant >2 fold up-regulation of ~4% (323) and down-regulation of ~1.5% (138) of the analyzed genes (qval <0.05, likelihood ratio test).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis in the current study.

claims.claim: The vast majority of affected genes changed within 2–10 fold upon SUMO depletion.
claims.source: However, the vast majority of affected genes changed within 2–10 fold, in stark contrast to dramatic ~1000 and~300 fold upregulation of R1 and R2 elements upon SUMO depletion (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis in the current study.

claims.claim: No significantly enriched GO terms associated with the up- and down- regulated gene sets upon SUMO KD were found related to nucleolar function and/or rRNA transcription.
claims.source: We did not find any significantly enriched GO terms associated with the up- and down- regulated gene sets upon SUMO KD related to nucleolar function and/or rRNA transcription (BH-adjusted p-value cutoff 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from GO enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: The only gene associated with the cellular component GO term 'nucleolus' among down-regulated genes was smt3 itself.
claims.source: Manual inspection showed that the only gene associated with the cellular component GO term 'nucleolus' ('GO:0005730') and offspring terms among down-regulated genes was smt3 itself.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from manual inspection of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Only two out of the 323 up-regulated genes - ph-p and CG9123 - are associated with the 'nucleolus' GO term.
claims.source: Only two out of the 323 up-regulated genes - ph-p and CG9123 - are associated with the 'nucleolus' GO term, however, neither of them has known function in rDNA expression.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from manual inspection of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: There is no direct indication that expression of genes involved in rDNA transcription and nucleolar function is affected by SUMO depletion.
claims.source: Therefore, while we cannot completely exclude a possibility of secondary effects of SUMO depletion, there is no direct indication that expression of genes involved in rDNA transcription and nucleolar function is affected by SUMO depletion.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the GO enrichment and manual inspection of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: SUMO plays direct role in rDNA silencing through modification of one or several proteins involved in rDNA expression.
claims.source: Several lines of evidence suggest that SUMO plays direct role in rDNA silencing through modification of one or several proteins involved in rDNA expression.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from multiple lines of evidence presented in the study.

claims.claim: Many nucleolar proteins, including several components of RNA pol I machinery and Udd protein, are SUMOylated in vivo.
claims.source: Second, our analysis of SUMOylated proteome using both targeted and unbiased approaches indicates that many nucleolar proteins, including several components of RNA pol I machinery and Udd protein previously implicated in rDNA expression (Zhang et al., 2014), are SUMOylated in vivo (Figure 6B, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from SUMOylation assays and proteomic analysis.

claims.claim: Recruitment of SUMO ligase Ubc9 to rDNA transgene led to its repression revealing direct effect of local SUMOylation on rDNA expression.
claims.source: Third, recruitment of SUMO ligase Ubc9 to rDNA transgene led to its repression revealing direct effect of local SUMOylation on rDNA expression (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the tethering experiment shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Local SUMOylation in proximity of gene promoters was shown to induce repression of Pol II driven transcription in Drosophila and mammals.
claims.source: Finally, local SUMOylation in proximity of gene promoters was shown to induce repression of Pol II driven transcription in Drosophila and mammals (Ninova et al., 2020a; Ninova et al., 2020b; Stielow et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2011; Lehembre et al., 2000; Yang et al., 2003; Yang and Sharrocks, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: SUMOylation at promoters is required for repression induced by KRAB-ZFPs, the largest family of mammalian transcriptional silencers.
claims.source: Particularly, SUMOylation at promoters is required for repression induced by KRAB-ZFPs, the largest family of mammalian transcriptional silencers (Li et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Li et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Pol I-driven rRNA promoters were found to be one of the most prominent sites of active sumoylation in human cells.
claims.source: Pol I-driven rRNA promoters were found to be one of the most prominent sites of active sumoylation in human cells (Neyret-Kahn et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Neyret-Kahn et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Inhibition of sumoylation caused upregulation of rRNA expression in human cells.
claims.source: Remarkably, inhibition of sumoylation caused upregulation of rRNA expression indicating that the role of SUMO in rDNA regulation is conserved between insects and mammals (Neyret-Kahn et al., 2013; Peng et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The role of SUMO in rDNA regulation is conserved between insects and mammals.
claims.source: Remarkably, inhibition of sumoylation caused upregulation of rRNA expression indicating that the role of SUMO in rDNA regulation is conserved between insects and mammals (Neyret-Kahn et al., 2013; Peng et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from observations in both Drosophila and human cells.

claims.claim: SUMOylation of chromatin-associated proteins might act as a molecular mark for rDNA repression.
claims.source: Our results suggest that SUMOylation of chromatin-associated proteins might act as a molecular mark for rDNA repression.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the study.

claims.claim: Repression might require modification of several chromatin-bound proteins rather than one specific target.
claims.source: However, modest R1/R2 upregulation observed upon depletion of several proteins suggest that repression might require modification of several chromatin-bound proteins rather than one specific target.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the RNAi screen results showing modest effects of individual protein knockdowns.

claims.claim: Promiscuous modification of multiple proteins is in line with the findings that SUMOylation consensus is very simple and quite common in the fly proteome.
claims.source: Promiscuous modification of multiple proteins is in line with the findings that SUMOylation consensus is very simple and quite common in the fly proteome (Nie et al., 2009) and our results that show that multiple nucleolar proteins are SUMOylated.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the computational analysis and SUMOylation assays.

claims.claim: The proposal that rDNA repression depend on cumulative SUMOylation of several proteins localized on rDNA is corroborated by studies in yeast that led to the ''SUMO spray'' hypothesis.
claims.source: The proposal that rDNA repression depend on cumulative SUMOylation of several proteins localized on rDNA corroborated by studies in yeast that led to the ''SUMO spray'' hypothesis (Psakhye and Jentsch, 2012) which suggests that SUMOylation of multiple proteins localized in physical proximity is required to induce downstream response in SUMO-dependent pathway.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to studies in yeast.

claims.claim: SUMOylation of multiple proteins localized in physical proximity is required to induce downstream response in SUMO-dependent pathway according to the SUMO spray hypothesis.
claims.source: The proposal that rDNA repression depend on cumulative SUMOylation of several proteins localized on rDNA corroborated by studies in yeast that led to the ''SUMO spray'' hypothesis (Psakhye and Jentsch, 2012) which suggests that SUMOylation of multiple proteins localized in physical proximity is required to induce downstream response in SUMO-dependent pathway.
claims.evidence: This is the SUMO spray hypothesis from yeast studies, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Multiple interactions between SUMOylated proteins and proteins that bind SUMO act synergistically.
claims.source: Importantly, multiple interactions between SUMOylated proteins and proteins that bind SUMO act synergistically and thus SUMOylation of any single protein is neither necessary nor sufficient to trigger downstream processes (Jentsch and Psakhye, 2013; Psakhye and Jentsch, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about SUMO spray mechanism, supported by citations.

claims.claim: SUMOylation of any single protein is neither necessary nor sufficient to trigger downstream processes in SUMO spray mechanism.
claims.source: Importantly, multiple interactions between SUMOylated proteins and proteins that bind SUMO act synergistically and thus SUMOylation of any single protein is neither necessary nor sufficient to trigger downstream processes (Jentsch and Psakhye, 2013; Psakhye and Jentsch, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about SUMO spray mechanism, supported by citations.

results.result: A single-unit rDNA transgene with a unique identification sequence (UID) inserted into the external transcribed spacer (ETS) can be expressed from a heterologous euchromatic genomic location and detected specifically by RT-qPCR and HCR-FISH.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C63 collectively demonstrate successful design and validation of the transgene system. RT-qPCR (C56-C59, Figure 1B) and HCR-FISH (C60-C62, Figure 1C) data confirm specific detection of transgene expression with appropriate controls (C57). The nuclear localization of transgene RNA (C61) is consistent with rRNA processing biology (C62).

results.result: Insertion of heterologous sequences (R1, R2 transposons, or CFP) into rDNA transgenes leads to 3- to 5-fold reduction in expression compared to intact transgenes, with the repressive effect not dependent on specific transposon sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C77 are supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2B showing consistent repression across different insertions. The experimental design controls for position effects by integrating all transgenes at the same genomic location (C70). The finding that CFP insertion causes similar repression to transposons (C73-C74) demonstrates sequence-independent repression.

results.result: Individual rDNA transgenes show high cell-to-cell variability in expression in nurse cells, with intact transgenes expressed in 67% of cells and interrupted transgenes in only 27% of cells, while control genes show uniform expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C93 are supported by HCR-FISH data in Figures 2C-E. The use of nurse cells from single egg chambers (C78-C79) provides an ideal system with genetically identical cells. Quantification shows both reduced fraction of expressing cells (C86-C87, Figure 2D) and reduced signal intensity (C88-C89, Figure 2E) for interrupted transgenes, while vasa control shows uniform expression (C81-C82, C90).

results.result: SUMO depletion causes dramatic and specific upregulation of R1 and R2 transposons (~1000-fold and ~300-fold respectively) in both germline and S2 cells, independent of the piRNA pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C109 are strongly supported by RNA-seq (Figure 3B-C) and RT-qPCR (Figure 3D-E) data. The specificity is demonstrated by comparison to other genes and transposons (C104-C105). Independence from piRNA pathway is shown by effects in S2 cells which lack piRNA machinery (C107-C109) and differential effects of Su(var)2-10 vs SUMO depletion (C99, C108).

results.result: SUMO depletion increases expression of both interrupted rDNA transgenes (50-54 fold) and intact transgenes (12-fold), equalizing their expression levels and demonstrating that SUMO is required for differential expression of intact versus interrupted rDNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C119 are supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 4A showing fold-changes upon SUMO knockdown. The key finding that intact and interrupted transgenes reach similar expression levels after SUMO depletion (C117, C118) demonstrates SUMO's role in discriminating between these rDNA types. The differential efficiency of repression (C119) is evident from the different fold-changes.

results.result: SUMO depletion eliminates cell-to-cell heterogeneity in rDNA transgene expression, with both intact and interrupted transgenes expressed in almost all nuclei at similarly high levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C124 are supported by HCR-FISH data in Figures 4B-D. The increase in fraction of expressing cells (C121, Figure 4C) and signal intensity per nucleus (C122, Figure 4D) demonstrate elimination of heterogeneity. The similar expression levels of intact and interrupted transgenes after SUMO depletion (C123-C124) confirm loss of discrimination.

results.result: SUMO depletion leads to 2.5-fold increase in endogenous pre-rRNA levels in both ovarian germ cells and S2 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126 are supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 4E showing consistent effects across cell types. This extends the transgene findings to endogenous rDNA arrays, though the magnitude of effect is smaller than for transgenes, possibly due to averaging across many rDNA units.

results.result: SUMO depletion causes 2.5- to 4-fold increase in RNA Pol I occupancy on intact and interrupted rDNA transgenes, indicating that SUMO-dependent repression acts at the transcriptional level.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C131 are supported by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 5A and Figure 5-supplement 1. The GFP-tagged Rpl135 localizes to nucleolus as expected (C127) and shows enrichment on rDNA (C128-C129). The increased Pol I occupancy upon SUMO depletion (C130) directly demonstrates transcriptional regulation (C131).

results.result: Endogenous rDNA units are enriched in H3K9me3 mark, but H3K9me3 levels do not change upon SUMO depletion, and transgenic rDNA has low H3K9me3 despite being SUMO-repressed, indicating H3K9me3 does not show clear correlation with SUMO-dependent silencing.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C140 are supported by ChIP-seq (Figure 5B) and ChIP-qPCR (Figures 5C-D) data. The lack of H3K9me3 change upon SUMO depletion (C134, C136, C139) despite increased expression, and the low H3K9me3 on repressed transgenes (C137-C138), demonstrate that H3K9me3 is not the primary mediator of SUMO-dependent repression (C140).

results.result: Knockdown of H3K9 methyltransferases induces only mild derepression of R1 and R2 (~2.5-fold for Su(var)3-9) compared to strong upregulation upon SUMO pathway knockdown (>1000-fold).
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C145 are supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 5E. The modest effect of H3K9 methyltransferase depletion (C143) compared to SUMO depletion (C145) indicates H3K9 methylation plays a minor role. The lack of redundancy among methyltransferases (C144) is demonstrated by similar effects of single and combined knockdowns.

results.result: Many nucleolar proteins including components of RNA Pol I machinery are SUMOylated, and SUMO is enriched on rDNA chromatin, suggesting SUMOylation of chromatin-associated proteins may mediate rDNA repression.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C157 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: SUMO ChIP-seq showing enrichment on rDNA (C150-C151, Figure 6A), SUMOylation assays detecting modification of Udd and CG3756 (C152-C153, Figure 6B), computational analysis showing high frequency of SUMOylation consensus in nucleolar proteins (C154-C155), and GO enrichment analysis (C156). However, C149 is speculative and should be noted as such.

results.result: RNAi screen identified five genes (Ulp1, CG13773, CG3756, Fib, mbm) whose knockdown increases R1/R2 expression, but with modest effects (3-30 fold) compared to SUMO depletion (>1000-fold), suggesting multiple proteins are involved in SUMO-dependent rDNA regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C163 are supported by RT-qPCR data from the RNAi screen in Figure 6C. The modest effects of individual protein knockdowns (C162) compared to SUMO depletion support the interpretation that multiple proteins contribute to repression (C163). However, C160 is speculative about mechanism.

results.result: Tethering of E2 SUMO ligase Ubc9 to rDNA transgene leads to 4.7-fold decrease in transgene expression, demonstrating that local SUMOylation can directly repress rDNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C164-C165 are supported by RT-qPCR data from the tethering experiment in Figure 6D. This provides direct evidence for local SUMOylation causing repression. However, the magnitude of repression is modest compared to the derepression upon SUMO depletion, which may indicate the tethering system has limitations or that additional factors are needed for full repression.

results.result: Individual rDNA units inserted in heterologous genomic positions outside native rDNA clusters can be transcribed by Pol I and processed, demonstrating that repeated structure and genomic location are not required for rDNA transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C170 and C174 are supported by the transgene expression data (Figures 1C, 2C, Figure 5-supplement 1) and agree with previous studies (C170 cites Karpen et al., 1988). The successful expression and processing of transgenic rDNA validates the experimental system and supports the conclusion about genomic location independence (C174).

results.result: Integration of heterologous sequences other than transposons can induce rDNA repression, and this appears to be an evolutionarily conserved process that prevents production of aberrant rRNA.
results.evaluation: Claim C178 is directly supported by the CFP insertion data (Figure 2B, claims C73-C74). Claim C180 is supported by the observation that 720 bp CFP is sufficient for repression. Claim C183 is an inference based on observations in both flies and mammals, though the evolutionary conservation aspect relies on cited literature rather than direct experimental evidence in this study.

results.result: Intact rDNA units also undergo silencing, albeit less frequently than interrupted units.
results.evaluation: Claim C184 is supported by HCR-FISH data showing intact transgenes are not expressed in all cells (67% vs 100%, Figure 2D, claims C86, C92). This demonstrates that silencing mechanisms affect both intact and interrupted rDNA, though with different efficiency.

results.result: SUMO plays a special role in repression of rDNA-targeting transposons independent of the piRNA pathway, and the same SUMO-dependent pathway is responsible for repression of both interrupted and intact rDNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C185-C190 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: dramatic R1/R2 upregulation upon SUMO depletion (C185, Figure 3), specificity compared to piRNA pathway and Su(var)2-10 effects (C186-C187), activation of both endogenous and transgenic rDNA (C188), and effects on both intact and interrupted transgenes (C189-C190, Figure 4).

results.result: SUMO-dependent repression correlates with levels of nascent pre-rRNA and Pol I occupancy, suggesting repression acts at the transcriptional level.
results.evaluation: Claims C191-C192 are supported by HCR-FISH data showing nascent RNA changes (Figure 4B-D) and ChIP data showing Pol I occupancy changes (Figure 5A). The correlation between these measurements supports the inference that repression acts transcriptionally (C192), though this is an inference rather than direct proof of mechanism.

results.result: Native rDNA units are enriched in H3K9me3, but the level remains high upon SUMO depletion, and transgenic rDNA is repressed despite low H3K9me3, indicating H3K9 methylation might contribute to rDNA silencing but cannot be the only component of SUMO-dependent repression.
results.evaluation: Claims C197-C201 are supported by ChIP data in Figure 5B-D. The disconnect between H3K9me3 levels and SUMO-dependent repression (C198-C199) supports the conclusion that H3K9me3 is not the primary mediator (C201), though it may play a contributory role (C200) as suggested by Su(var)3-9 knockdown effects.

results.result: SUMO depletion causes changes in gene expression affecting ~4% of genes with >2-fold upregulation and ~1.5% with downregulation, but no significant enrichment of nucleolar or rRNA transcription-related genes, suggesting SUMO's effect on rDNA is not mediated by indirect effects on gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C204-C210 are supported by RNA-seq analysis and GO enrichment analysis. The lack of enrichment for nucleolar/rRNA-related genes (C207-C209) and the modest fold-changes for most genes (C206) compared to dramatic R1/R2 upregulation support the conclusion of direct SUMO action (C210). However, the possibility of indirect effects cannot be completely excluded as acknowledged in the text.

results.result: Multiple lines of evidence suggest SUMO plays a direct role in rDNA silencing through modification of proteins involved in rDNA expression, including SUMOylation of nucleolar proteins and direct repression by tethered Ubc9.
results.evaluation: Claims C211-C213 are supported by: SUMOylation of nucleolar proteins including Pol I components (C212, Figure 6B), and tethering experiments showing direct repression (C213, Figure 6D). These provide strong evidence for direct SUMO action, though the specific target proteins remain to be fully identified.

results.result: The role of SUMO in rDNA regulation is conserved between insects and mammals.
results.evaluation: Claim C218 is supported by citations to studies in human cells showing similar effects of SUMO inhibition on rRNA expression (C217, citing Neyret-Kahn et al., 2013; Peng et al., 2019). However, this relies on literature rather than direct experimental evidence in the current study.

results.result: SUMOylation of chromatin-associated proteins might act as a molecular mark for rDNA repression, potentially through cumulative SUMOylation of multiple proteins (SUMO spray hypothesis) rather than modification of a single specific target.
results.evaluation: Claims C219-C225 are largely speculative (C219, C220, C222 are explicitly speculation/inference). While the SUMO spray hypothesis from yeast (C222-C225) provides a conceptual framework, and the modest effects of individual protein knockdowns (C220) are consistent with this model, direct evidence for SUMO spray mechanism in rDNA regulation is lacking. This represents a proposed model rather than a demonstrated result.
